claim: Enhanced synchronization of neural activity in the beta band (13–30 Hz) has been consistently observed in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in patients with Parkinson's disease.
source: Enhanced synchronization of neural activity in the beta band (13–30 Hz) has been consistently observed in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in patients with Parkinson's disease (Kühn et al., 2009; Neumann et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies (Kühn et al., 2009; Neumann et al., 2016).

claim: Synchrony in the beta frequency band takes the form of short-lived bursts of different durations and amplitudes.
source: Synchrony in this frequency band takes the form of short-lived bursts of different durations and amplitudes (Tinkhauser et al., 2017a; Tinkhauser et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies (Tinkhauser et al., 2017a; Tinkhauser et al., 2017b).

claim: The occurrence rate of longer beta bursts with large amplitude positively correlates with motor impairment.
source: The occurrence rate of longer beta bursts with large amplitude positively correlates with motor impairment (Tinkhauser et al., 2017a; Tinkhauser et al., 2020; Torrecillos et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies (Tinkhauser et al., 2017a; Tinkhauser et al., 2020; Torrecillos et al., 2018).

claim: Closed-loop deep brain stimulation (DBS), which selectively truncates long duration beta bursts, can achieve clinical improvement that is at least as good as that with conventional continuous DBS in acute trials.
source: Closed-loop deep brain stimulation (DBS), which selectively truncates long duration beta bursts, can achieve clinical improvement that is at least as good as that with conventional continuous DBS in acute trials (Little et al., 2013; Little et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies (Little et al., 2013; Little et al., 2016).

claim: Parkinsonian patients have been shown to be capable of voluntarily regulating STN beta-band power measured from electrodes implanted for DBS.
source: Parkinsonian patients have been shown to be capable of voluntarily regulating STN beta-band power measured from electrodes implanted for DBS (Carney, 2019; He et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies (Carney, 2019; He et al., 2019).

claim: It is still not clear whether modulating beta oscillations in STN through neurofeedback training can lead to changes in motor performance in patients with Parkinson's disease.
source: However, it is still not clear whether modulating beta oscillations in STN through neurofeedback training can lead to changes in motor performance in patients with Parkinson's disease (Subramanian et al., 2011; Erickson-Davis et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies (Subramanian et al., 2011; Erickson-Davis et al., 2012) that indicate uncertainty in the field.

claim: Reduced activities in the beta band and increases in power in the tremor frequency band, corresponding to the theta band (3–7 Hz), in the STN, as well as reduced basal ganglia-cortical coherence in the beta frequency band have been observed during the presence of resting tremor in Parkinson's disease.
source: For example, reduced activities in the beta band and increases in power in the tremor frequency band, corresponding to the theta band (3–7 Hz), in the STN, as well as reduced basal ganglia-cortical coherence in the beta frequency band have been observed during the presence of resting tremor in Parkinson's disease (Hirschmann et al., 2013; Qasim et al., 2016; Asch et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies (Hirschmann et al., 2013; Qasim et al., 2016; Asch et al., 2020).

claim: One in five patients shows resurgence of tremor if DBS is only switched on when STN beta activity is high.
source: Moreover, one in five patients shows resurgence of tremor if DBS is only switched on when STN beta activity is high (Little and Brown, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study (Little and Brown, 2020).

claim: Healthy young participants can suppress cortical beta measured using electroencephalogram (EEG) with veritable neurofeedback better than sham feedback.
source: In a recent study, we showed that healthy young participants can indeed suppress cortical beta measured using electroencephalogram (EEG) with veritable neurofeedback better than sham feedback (He et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study (He et al., 2020).

claim: Twelve Parkinsonian patients, who underwent bilateral implantation of DBS electrodes targeting the motor area of the STN, participated in this study during the time when the DBS leads were temporarily externalized.
source: Twelve Parkinsonian patients, who underwent bilateral implantation of DBS electrodes targeting the motor area of the STN, participated in this study during the time when the DBS leads were temporarily externalized.
evidence: The claim describes the study participants and is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: The final basketball position was higher in the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition (t20 = 4.6054, p = 0.0002).
source: Paired t-test showed that the final basketball position was higher in the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition (t20 = 4.6054, p = 0.0002, Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (paired t-test) of experimental data and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Neurofeedback control was not consequent on physical movement that was monitored by EMGs attached to both forearms of the participants.
source: and this was not consequent on physical movement that was monitored by EMGs attached to both forearms of the participants (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMG data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neurofeedback training led to reduced accumulated beta burst duration in the STN LFPs (t20 = −4.7415, p = 0.0001, 17.40 ± 1.44% compared to 22.43 ± 1.85%).
source: The neurofeedback training also led to reduced accumulated beta burst duration in the STN LFPs determined as percentage of time with beta amplitude being over the predefined threshold (t20 = −4.7415, p = 0.0001, 17.40 ± 1.44% compared to 22.43 ± 1.85%, mean ± SEM, Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Neurofeedback training led to a reduced average burst duration (t20 = −3.9428, p = 0.0008, 319.6 ± 19.3 ms compared to 377.2 ± 21.5 ms).
source: a reduced average burst duration (t20 = −3.9428, p = 0.0008, 319.6 ± 19.3 ms compared to 377.2 ± 21.5 ms, Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Neurofeedback training led to a reduced number of bursts per second (t20 = −4.8536, p = 0.0001, 0.446 ± 0.030 compared to 0.531 ± 0.033).
source: and a reduced number of bursts per second (t20 = −4.8536, p = 0.0001, 0.446 ± 0.030 compared to 0.531 ± 0.033, Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The bursts with durations longer than 400 ms were reduced more consistently compared with the shorter bursts.
source: The bursts with durations longer than 400 ms were reduced more consistently compared with the shorter bursts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increase in the broad gamma frequency band (55–95 Hz) in the STN LFPs was observed (t20 = 3.4899, p = 0.0023).
source: In addition, we observed an increase in the broad gamma frequency band (55–95 Hz) in the STN LFPs (t20 = 3.4899, p = 0.0023, Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: There was no significant change in the gamma activities in the EEG measured over the motor cortex (z = 0.7821, p = 0.4342).
source: There was no significant change in the gamma activities in the EEG measured over the motor cortex (z = 0.7821, p = 0.4342).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The phase synchrony index between the conditioned STN and ipsilateral motor cortex was significantly reduced in the beta band in the 'Training' condition compared with the 'No Training' condition (t20 = −2.5462, p = 0.0192).
source: The phase synchrony index (t20 = −2.5462, p = 0.0192, Figure 4I) and spectral coherence (z = −3.1803, p = 0.0015, Figure 4J) between the conditioned STN and ipsilateral motor cortex were significantly reduced in the beta band in the 'Training' condition compared with the 'No Training' condition
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 4I.

claim: The spectral coherence between the conditioned STN and ipsilateral motor cortex was significantly reduced in the beta band in the 'Training' condition compared with the 'No Training' condition (z = −3.1803, p = 0.0015).
source: The phase synchrony index (t20 = −2.5462, p = 0.0192, Figure 4I) and spectral coherence (z = −3.1803, p = 0.0015, Figure 4J) between the conditioned STN and ipsilateral motor cortex were significantly reduced in the beta band in the 'Training' condition compared with the 'No Training' condition
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 4J.

claim: There was a sustained carry-over effect of neurofeedback training over the short time window (~2 s) after the neurofeedback phase when a black screen was presented before the Go cue.
source: There was a sustained carry-over effect of neurofeedback training over the short time window (~2 s) after the neurofeedback phase when a black screen was presented before the Go cue.
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling results showing correlations between measurements during feedback and pre-cue periods.

claim: The average normalized beta power during the 2 s pre-Go cue was positively correlated with the average normalized beta power during the 4 s feedback phase (k = 0.6050 ± 0.0241, p < 0.0001).
source: The average normalized beta power (k = 0.6050 ± 0.0241, p < 0.0001), accumulated beta burst duration (k = 0.0892 ± 0.0144, p < 0.0001), and normalized gamma power (k = 0.9617 ± 0.0073, p < 0.0001) during the 2 s pre-Go cue were positively correlated with the average normalized beta power, beta burst duration, and normalized gamma power during the 4 s feedback phase, respectively, as identified by the generalized linear mixed effects (GLME) modeling
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: The average beta power during the 2 s pre-Go cue was significantly reduced in the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition (k = −0.2523 ± 0.0769, p = 0.0011).
source: If we replaced the predictor by the experimental condition ('Training' or 'No Training') in the models, the results revealed that the average beta power (k = −0.2523 ± 0.0769, p = 0.0011) and accumulated beta burst duration (k = −0.0601 ± 0.0172, p = 0.0005) during the 2 s pre-Go cue were significantly reduced in the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: The accumulated beta burst duration during the 2 s pre-Go cue was significantly reduced in the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition (k = −0.0601 ± 0.0172, p = 0.0005).
source: If we replaced the predictor by the experimental condition ('Training' or 'No Training') in the models, the results revealed that the average beta power (k = −0.2523 ± 0.0769, p = 0.0011) and accumulated beta burst duration (k = −0.0601 ± 0.0172, p = 0.0005) during the 2 s pre-Go cue were significantly reduced in the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: The average gamma power during the 2 s pre-Go cue was significantly increased in the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition (k = 0.0781 ± 0.0296, p = 0.0083).
source: In contrast, the average gamma power during the 2 s pre-Go cue were significantly increased (k = 0.0781 ± 0.0296, p = 0.0083) in the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: The reaction time in response to the Go cue was significantly reduced in the 'Training' condition compared with the 'No Training' condition (487.4 ± 29.7 ms compared to 510.9 ± 32.3 ms, t20 = −2.7518, p = 0.0123).
source: The reaction time in response to the Go cue was significantly reduced in the 'Training' condition compared with the 'No Training' condition (487.4 ± 29.7 ms compared to 510.9 ± 32.3 ms, t20 = −2.7518, p = 0.0123, paired t-test, Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 6A.

claim: STN average beta power during the 2s before the Go-cue significantly contributed to the prediction of reaction time.
source: When STN average beta power or beta burst characteristics (average burst duration, accumulated burst duration) during the 2s before the Go-cue were used as the only predictor in separate models, all of them significantly contributed to the prediction of reaction time (Models 1–5, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling results shown in Table 2.

claim: Beta burst characteristics (average burst duration, accumulated burst duration) during the 2s before the Go-cue significantly contributed to the prediction of reaction time.
source: When STN average beta power or beta burst characteristics (average burst duration, accumulated burst duration) during the 2s before the Go-cue were used as the only predictor in separate models, all of them significantly contributed to the prediction of reaction time (Models 1–5, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling results shown in Table 2.

claim: Around 20% of the variance in the reaction time was being explained by Model 6 (R2 = 0.2072).
source: Overall, around 20% of the variance in the reaction time was being explained by the model (Model 6, R2 = 0.2072, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the R-squared value from GLME modeling.

claim: There was no significant difference in the RT between the selected trials from the 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions with matched normalized beta power (t20 = −0.4374, p = 0.6665).
source: The results showed no significant difference in the RT (t20 = −0.4374, p = 0.6665, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) nor in the normalized gamma power (z = −0.8168, p = 0.4140, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) between the selected trials from the 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions but with matched normalized beta power.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of a subset of experimental data with matched beta power.

claim: There was no significant difference in the normalized gamma power between the selected trials from the 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions with matched normalized beta power (z = −0.8168, p = 0.4140).
source: The results showed no significant difference in the RT (t20 = −0.4374, p = 0.6665, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) nor in the normalized gamma power (z = −0.8168, p = 0.4140, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) between the selected trials from the 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions but with matched normalized beta power.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of a subset of experimental data with matched beta power.

claim: Beta modulation during neurofeedback training contributes to the changes in RT.
source: Overall these analyses suggest that beta modulation during neurofeedback training does contribute to the changes in RT, even though other condition factors (e.g., cognitive requirement) may also contribute to the observed difference in the RT between the 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis showing that matched beta power eliminates RT differences between conditions.

claim: Five out of the twelve participants (nine STN hemispheres) in the study displayed resting tremor during the recording.
source: Five out of the twelve participants (nine STN hemispheres) in the study displayed resting tremor during the recording, which enabled us to investigate how volitional suppression of STN beta oscillations affected tremor in Parkinson's disease.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the study participants.

claim: The tremor severity increased during the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition contralateral to seven out of the tested nine hemispheres (t8 = 3.2589, p = 0.0115).
source: The tremor severity, quantified based on the measurements from the tri-axial accelerometer attached to the contralateral hand, increased during the 'Training' condition compared to the 'No Training' condition contralateral to seven out of the tested nine hemispheres (Figure 6C, t8 = 3.2589, p = 0.0115).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of accelerometer data and reference to Figure 6C.

claim: A significantly positive correlation was observed between the tremor power and the theta band power in the STN LFP across hemispheres (R = 0.5003, p = 0.034).
source: In addition, a significantly positive correlation was observed between the tremor power and the theta band power in the STN LFP across hemispheres (R = 0.5003, p = 0.034, Pearson's, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pearson's correlation analysis and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant difference in the tremor severity between 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions when 75% of trials with matched normalized beta power from the two conditions were considered (t8 = −1.1152, p = 0.2971).
source: There was no significant difference in the tremor severity between 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions when 75% of trials with matched normalized beta power from the two conditions were considered (t8 = −1.1152, p = 0.2971, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of a subset of experimental data with matched beta power.

claim: The difference in the experimental condition by itself did not lead to significant difference in the tremor severity between the 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions if the beta power was the same.
source: These results suggested that the difference in the experimental condition by itself did not lead to significant difference in the tremor severity between the 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions if the beta power was the same.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis showing no tremor difference when beta power is matched.

claim: Four participants (eight hemispheres) repeated the task on two separate, consecutive days.
source: In this study, four participants (eight hemispheres) repeated the task on two separate, consecutive days.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Six out of the eight tested hemispheres showed increased neurofeedback control on Day 2 compared to Day 1.
source: Comparing against Day 1, six out of the eight tested hemispheres showed increased neurofeedback control (indicated by the increased difference in the 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions) on Day 2 (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: GLME modeling confirmed a significant interaction between experimental condition and recording days on the basketball's final position (k = 0.1497 ± 0.0372, p = 0.0001).
source: GLME modeling using the difference in the basketball's final position, average beta power, or accumulated beta burst duration between 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions as dependent variable, experimental day (Day 1 or Day 2) as fixed predictor, and a random intercept for each hemisphere confirmed a significant interaction between experimental condition and recording days on the basketball's final position (k = 0.1497 ± 0.0372, p = 0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: GLME modeling confirmed a significant interaction between experimental condition and recording days on average beta power (k = −12.56 ± 3.8987, p = 0.0017).
source: GLME modeling using the difference in the basketball's final position, average beta power, or accumulated beta burst duration between 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions as dependent variable, experimental day (Day 1 or Day 2) as fixed predictor, and a random intercept for each hemisphere confirmed a significant interaction between experimental condition and recording days on the basketball's final position (k = 0.1497 ± 0.0372, p = 0.0001), average beta power (k = −12.56 ± 3.8987, p = 0.0017)
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: GLME modeling confirmed a significant interaction between experimental condition and recording days on accumulated beta burst duration (k = −0.1803 ± 0.0632, p = 0.0051).
source: GLME modeling using the difference in the basketball's final position, average beta power, or accumulated beta burst duration between 'Training' and 'No Training' conditions as dependent variable, experimental day (Day 1 or Day 2) as fixed predictor, and a random intercept for each hemisphere confirmed a significant interaction between experimental condition and recording days on the basketball's final position (k = 0.1497 ± 0.0372, p = 0.0001), average beta power (k = −12.56 ± 3.8987, p = 0.0017), and accumulated beta burst duration (k = −0.1803 ± 0.0632, p = 0.0051)
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant change in the baseline beta power during rest between Day 1 and Day 2.
source: There was no significant change in the baseline beta power during rest between Day 1 and Day 2 (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: GLME modeling confirmed a significant interaction between experimental day and average beta power (k = −0.1949, p = 0.0108), which could not be explained by the different experimental conditions.
source: Apart from the significant interaction between experimental condition and the average beta power (k = −0.5835, p < 0.0001), the results also confirmed a significant interaction between experimental day and average beta power (k = −0.1949, p = 0.0108), which could not be explained by the different experimental conditions, suggesting a baseline reduction of the beta power over the two consecutive training days.
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: There was a baseline reduction of the beta power over the two consecutive training days.
source: Apart from the significant interaction between experimental condition and the average beta power (k = −0.5835, p < 0.0001), the results also confirmed a significant interaction between experimental day and average beta power (k = −0.1949, p = 0.0108), which could not be explained by the different experimental conditions, suggesting a baseline reduction of the beta power over the two consecutive training days.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GLME modeling results showing a day effect on beta power.

claim: There was no significant baseline change in accumulated beta burst duration over the two consecutive training days (k = 0.0041, p = 0.8996).
source: There was no significant baseline change if we replaced average beta power by accumulated beta burst duration in the model (k = 0.0041, p = 0.8996).
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling of experimental data.

claim: For the two patients (four hemispheres) who had tremor and repeated the task over two consecutive days, tremor during the 'Training' condition was increased more on Day 2 than Day 1 in all four hemispheres.
source: For the two patients (four hemispheres) who had tremor and repeated the task over two consecutive days, tremor during the 'Training' condition was increased more on Day 2 than Day 1 in all four hemispheres (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The reduced beta and increased theta power in the STN during neurofeedback training on Day 2 associated with the increased tremor.
source: suggesting the reduced beta and increased theta power in the STN during neurofeedback training on Day 2 associated with the increased tremor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GLME modeling results showing effects of beta and theta on tremor.

claim: This is the first study to show that volitional suppression of beta bursts in the STN LFP facilitated by neurofeedback training is able to speed up movement initiation in subsequent cued movement in Parkinsonian patients.
source: This is the first study to show that volitional suppression of beta bursts in the STN LFP facilitated by neurofeedback training is able to speed up movement initiation in subsequent cued movement in Parkinsonian patients.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the study's main finding, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: The suppression of beta was accompanied by an increase in the broad gamma band activity in the STN.
source: We also showed that the suppression of beta was accompanied by an increase in the broad gamma band activity in the STN.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing increased gamma activity during neurofeedback training.

claim: Both the reduced beta and increased gamma in the STN LFP before the Go-cue predicted faster reaction time.
source: Both the reduced beta and increased gamma in the STN LFP before the Go-cue predicted faster reaction time.
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling results showing both beta and gamma effects on reaction time.

claim: The increase of gamma and reduction of beta band activity in STN have been reported during voluntary movements.
source: The increase of gamma and reduction of beta band activity in STN have been reported during voluntary movements (Androulidakis et al., 2007; Kempf et al., 2009; Brücke et al., 2012; Brücke et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The level of gamma increase and beta reduction during the onset of voluntary gripping movements helps predict gripping force and movement speed.
source: The level of gamma increase and beta reduction during the onset of voluntary gripping movements also helps predict gripping force and movement speed (Tan et al., 2016; Lofredi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: In the dopamine-depleted state, movement-related subcortical gamma power significantly decreased.
source: In the dopamine-depleted state, movement-related subcortical gamma power significantly decreased (Kempf et al., 2009; Litvak et al., 2012), particularly during the trials when peak velocity was slower than ON medication (Lofredi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Reduced subcortical gamma signaling in the dopamine-depleted state may contribute to bradykinesia.
source: These studies suggest that in addition to increased synchrony in the beta band, reduced subcortical gamma signaling in the dopamine-depleted state may also contribute to bradykinesia.
evidence: The claim is inferred from previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Parkinsonian patients were able to purposely increase subcortical gamma band activities.
source: The present study shows that Parkinsonian patients were able to purposely increase subcortical gamma band activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing increased gamma during neurofeedback training.

claim: STN gamma activity increased during motor imagery and scaled with imagined gripping force.
source: The observed effect in the gamma frequency band may have been mediated by the mental strategy or arousal, since a previous study has shown that STN gamma activity increased during motor imagery and scaled with imagined gripping force (Fischer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Increases in gamma oscillations before the Go-cue predict faster reaction time, over and above the prediction afforded by reduced beta band activities.
source: We also showed that increases in gamma oscillations before the Go-cue predict faster reaction time, over and above the prediction afforded by reduced beta band activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by GLME modeling results showing independent effects of gamma and beta on reaction time.

claim: Gamma oscillations may be another important treatment target for Parkinson's disease.
source: These results suggest that gamma oscillations may be another important treatment target for Parkinson's disease.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the study's findings about gamma's role in motor performance.

claim: Treatments increasing subcortical gamma oscillations, such as medication with levodopa, may help improve motor initiation.
source: Treatments increasing subcortical gamma oscillations, such as medication with levodopa (Androulidakis et al., 2007), may also help improve motor initiation.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the study's findings, with a citation to support the effect of levodopa on gamma.

claim: Neurofeedback training targeting beta oscillations may increase tremor, as well as tremor band activities in the STN LFP in tremulous patients.
source: Another important observation in this study is that neurofeedback training targeting beta oscillations may increase tremor, as well as tremor band activities in the STN LFP in tremulous patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing increased tremor during neurofeedback training.

claim: In the presence of tremor, neuronal oscillations at tremor frequency (3–7 Hz) tend to increase in the cortical-basal ganglia-thalamic circuit.
source: Our results are consistent with previous studies showing that, in the presence of tremor, neuronal oscillations at tremor frequency (3–7 Hz) tend to increase in the cortical-basal ganglia-thalamic circuit (Hirschmann et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: In the presence of tremor, beta power (13–30 Hz) and beta band coupling in the motor network are reduced.
source: Our results are consistent with previous studies showing that, in the presence of tremor, neuronal oscillations at tremor frequency (3–7 Hz) tend to increase in the cortical-basal ganglia-thalamic circuit (Hirschmann et al., 2013), whereas beta power (13–30 Hz) and beta band coupling in the motor network are reduced (Qasim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Neurofeedback training targeting beta activity might not help patients with tremor.
source: Therefore, neurofeedback training targeting beta activity might not help patients with tremor.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the study's findings that beta suppression increases tremor.

claim: Patients with tremor might be better served by neurofeedback training focusing on tremor-related oscillations.
source: Such patients might be better served by neurofeedback training focusing on tremor-related oscillations.
evidence: The claim is a speculative suggestion based on the study's findings.

claim: The patients' ability to modulate their STN beta activity during the neurofeedback phase increased in Day 2 compared to Day 1.
source: We showed that the patients' ability to modulate their STN beta activity during the neurofeedback phase increased in Day 2 compared to Day 1, even though the baseline beta activities during rest were similar during Day 1 and Day 2.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data comparing performance across two days.

claim: The baseline beta activities during rest were similar during Day 1 and Day 2.
source: We showed that the patients' ability to modulate their STN beta activity during the neurofeedback phase increased in Day 2 compared to Day 1, even though the baseline beta activities during rest were similar during Day 1 and Day 2.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Spaced training may facilitate further learning.
source: These results suggest that spaced training may facilitate further learning.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the improved performance on Day 2.

claim: It remains to be tested if spaced training across multiple sessions would attenuate the connections in the targeted neural network that give rise to synchronization through Hebbian plasticity.
source: However, it also remains to be tested if spaced training across multiple sessions would attenuate the connections in the targeted neural network that give rise to synchronization through Hebbian plasticity (Legenstein et al., 2008; Ros et al., 2014) and whether spaced training can lead to reduced beta synchrony even during rest outside of the neurofeedback task.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about future research directions, with citations to relevant theoretical frameworks.

claim: Veritable neurofeedback is better than sham feedback in training participants to modulate neural activities even when using similar self-reported mental strategies.
source: In a separate study with young healthy participants, we showed that 'veritable feedback' is better than 'sham feedback' in training participants to modulate neural activities even when using similar self-reported mental strategies (He et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: With the current study, we cannot disambiguate whether the observed effects are due to the neurofeedback training or mediated by mental strategy (motor imagery).
source: Therefore, with the current study, we cannot disambiguate whether the observed effects are due to the neurofeedback training or mediated by mental strategy (motor imagery).
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the study design.

claim: Parkinsonian patients can purposely modulate pathological subcortical brain activities.
source: However, the main results remain valid: Parkinsonian patients can purposely modulate pathological subcortical brain activities, and this modulation led to improved movement initialization.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing successful neurofeedback control.

claim: Modulation of pathological subcortical brain activities led to improved movement initialization.
source: However, the main results remain valid: Parkinsonian patients can purposely modulate pathological subcortical brain activities, and this modulation led to improved movement initialization.
